requirements: The core contributions of Blink — a CPU-free LLM inference architecture that redistributes serving responsibilities across a SmartNIC DPU and a GPU-resident persistent scheduler — have been reproduced, including its latency, throughput, interference-resilience, and energy-efficiency claims across four models and three baseline serving systems.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware and software environment described in Table 5 and §5 has been provisioned: an H100 GPU host paired with a BlueField-3 DPU over a 200 Gbps RDMA link, running the specified CUDA/DOCA/TensorRT toolchain, with DVFS disabled and the required kernel/OS configuration.

The host server has been provisioned with the exact hardware specified in Table 5 (GPU, CPU, DRAM, host NIC), which serves as the compute backend for Blink and as the baseline machine for TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang.

Code has been implemented that verifies the host CPU configuration matches Table 5: two Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y sockets providing 96 cores total at a 2.40 GHz nominal base frequency (24 cores/socket × 2 sockets, with hyper-threading accounted for).

A separate BlueField-3 DPU machine has been provisioned that hosts the Blink frontend (§4.4, Table 5), providing the ARM cores and memory needed to run the tokenizer, HTTP+SSE server, and RDMA orchestrator.

Code has been implemented that verifies the DPU has at least 32 GB of onboard memory available to ARM-side processes, matching the DPU specification in Table 5.

Code has been implemented that installs TensorRT v10.14 as the underlying execution backend used by both TensorRT-LLM and Blink.

Code and configuration ensure that the TensorRT engine artifacts consumed by the TensorRT-LLM baseline are byte-identical (or content-hash equivalent) to the engines loaded by Blink, so that any performance delta reflects orchestration only.
TensorRT-LLM runtime configuration enables CUDA Graphs and explicitly disables chunked prefill, prefix caching, and CPU offloading, matching the paper's production baseline settings.

vLLM runtime configuration enables CUDA Graphs, uses fp16 precision with paged attention, and explicitly disables chunked prefill, prefix caching, and CPU offloading via engine arguments.
Code has been implemented that launches vLLM on the same H100 server with the workload generator connected via the same 10 Gbps switch as TensorRT-LLM and SGLang.

Code has been implemented that launches SGLang on the same H100 server with the workload generator connected via the same 10 Gbps switch as the other baselines.

Configuration ensures that the CPU cores available to the baselines match the paper's setup (six reserved for inference under interference conditions per NVIDIA guidelines) and that DVFS remains disabled with governor=performance as in Table 5.

A negative-control assertion has been implemented that verifies at startup that each baseline's effective configuration reports chunked_prefill=disabled, prefix_caching=disabled, and CPU offloading=disabled, and fails the run if any of these are enabled.
Behavioral and structural checks confirm that each configured baseline runs end-to-end and that TensorRT-LLM shares Blink's engines rather than a re-compiled variant.

An integration test has been implemented that sends a fixed ShareGPT prompt through each of TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang and asserts that a non-empty completion is returned with token-per-second telemetry logged.
A test has been implemented that computes the SHA-256 hash of the TensorRT engine files loaded by the TensorRT-LLM baseline and by Blink at runtime and asserts they are equal per model.
A test has been implemented that parses the runtime configuration reported by TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang and asserts that CUDA Graphs are marked enabled in the effective server configuration.

Blink's backend has been implemented per §4.2: a persistent CUDA scheduler kernel (single thread block, 256 threads) performing parallel slot scanning, atomic CAS claiming, continuous batching with pause-and-resume inline prefill, FCFS policy, on-device token sampling, the ring-buffer lifecycle state machine, the paged KV-cache manager, and the (batch, seq-len) precomputed CUDA graph cache built on TensorRT engines.

The persistent GPU scheduler kernel that replaces the host-driven decode loop has been implemented with its structural properties, control loop, parallel scanning, and the demonstrated speedup over an otherwise identical CPU-resident scheduler.
The kernel structural properties described in §4.2 have been realized in code.
Code has been implemented that launches a single persistent CUDA kernel once at startup and lets it run indefinitely to serve inference, without launching a new kernel per decode step.
The persistent scheduler kernel occupies exactly one CUDA thread block (grid dimension = 1).
The persistent scheduler thread block is configured with exactly 256 threads as stated in §4.2.
The scheduler kernel never yields to the host during steady-state operation; the implementation contains no host-side synchronization or CPU-mediated bookkeeping on the token-critical path.
The five-step control loop enumerated in §4.2 has been implemented inside the persistent kernel.
The scheduler loop scans the ring buffer for newly submitted prompts on every iteration (step 1 of the control loop).
The scheduler claims pending prompt slots via atomic compare-and-swap on the slot state field (step 2 of the control loop).
The scheduler selects and launches the appropriate CUDA graph for either prefill or decode based on the current batch state (step 3 of the control loop).
The scheduler polls device-resident output buffers to detect completion of token sampling (step 4 of the control loop).
The scheduler publishes generated tokens and updated per-slot status back to the ring buffer at the end of each iteration (step 5 of the control loop).
Parallel slot scanning across the 256 scheduler threads has been implemented and meets the stated timing bound.
All 256 scheduler threads scan disjoint contiguous ranges of ring-buffer slots in parallel, so that no single thread traverses the full 4096-slot buffer serially.
Slot claiming is lock-free and requires no inter-block synchronization; only atomic CAS on slot state fields is used to coordinate between threads.
Measured on the H100 testbed, a complete parallel scan of all 4096 ring-buffer slots by the scheduler completes within the 1 µs–5 µs range reported in §4.2.

The controlled Figure 3 comparison between GPU-resident and CPU-resident scheduling (Qwen3-32B, FP16, H100, batch size 16, same scheduling policy) has been implemented and yields the reported normalized makespans.
Both the GPU-resident and CPU-resident scheduler variants share an identical scheduling policy and run against the same compiled TensorRT engine so that only the scheduler placement differs.
In the CPU-resident baseline, sampled tokens are copied from GPU to host memory over PCIe after each decode step, and the batch is reassembled on the CPU before launching the next graph.
Token sampling is performed on the GPU in both scheduler placements, matching the practice of popular CPU-centric systems such as vLLM.
On the 32 requests × 64 input → 32 output configuration (Figure 3), the CPU-resident scheduler's normalized makespan relative to the GPU-resident scheduler is measured to be approximately 1.70×.
On the 32 requests × 256 input → 256 output configuration (Figure 3), the CPU-resident scheduler's normalized makespan relative to the GPU-resident scheduler is measured to be approximately 1.26×.
On the 32 requests × 512 input → 1024 output configuration (Figure 3), the CPU-resident scheduler's normalized makespan relative to the GPU-resident scheduler is measured to be approximately 1.16×.
On the 64 requests × 256 input → 256 output configuration (Figure 3), the CPU-resident scheduler's normalized makespan relative to the GPU-resident scheduler is measured to be approximately 1.22×.

Across all four Figure 3 workload configurations, the CPU-resident scheduler inflates total makespan versus the GPU-resident scheduler within the paper's reported 1.16×–1.70× range, with the largest penalty appearing on the shortest-output workload where per-step PCIe round-trip overhead dominates.
Continuous batching with FCFS policy and pause-and-resume inline prefill has been implemented inside the persistent scheduler.
The scheduler orders admission and step selection using a first-come-first-served policy, matching TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang.
The scheduler implements continuous batching semantics (new requests may enter the running batch mid-generation) rather than static batching.
While a decode graph executes asynchronously, the 256 scheduler threads scan the ring buffer in parallel for pending prompts so that scan latency is hidden behind decode compute.

Before pausing decode to admit new prefills, the scheduler evaluates all three conditions from §4.2 (pending prefills, free batch-slot capacity, and fire-and-forget launch-window headroom) and only pauses when all three hold.
The batch-slot capacity check accounts for slots that will complete during the current step (not just currently-free slots).
The launch-window headroom check verifies that enough fire-and-forget budget remains for both the prefill graph and the resumed decode graph before pausing.

Once the three conditions hold, the scheduler pauses in-flight decode requests after the current step, executes a prefill graph for the new arrivals, merges the newly prefilled requests into the decode batch, and restarts the decode loop.
The entire pause-and-resume prefill admission occurs within a single persistent kernel invocation, without any host round-trip between decode and prefill.
New requests are admitted within one decode step's latency, bounding TTFT without sacrificing decode throughput.
The GPU-resident ring buffer and its per-slot lifecycle state machine described in §4.2 have been implemented.
The ring buffer resides in GPU (HBM) memory and is the sole shared data structure between the DPU frontend and the GPU backend.
The ring buffer is laid out as a fixed set of slots plus shared arenas for input tokens and generated tokens; slots carry offsets into the token arenas rather than inline token data.
Each slot records per-request metadata including prompt identity, token counts, and generation progress, in a layout compatible with one-sided RDMA reads/writes from the DPU.
The full slot lifecycle state machine enumerated in §4.2 is present.
The state machine defines an empty state used for free/available slots.
The state machine defines a prefill_pending state used after the DPU has written a prompt but before the scheduler claims it.
The state machine defines a prefill_processing state used while the prefill graph is executing for that slot.
The state machine defines a decode_processing state used while the slot participates in ongoing decode iterations.
The state machine defines a decode_completed state used once the slot has produced its final token and is ready for detokenization/reclaim.
The state machine defines a decode_paused state used to support preemption during pause-and-resume continuous batching.
Ownership transfers and state transitions between DPU and GPU are performed exclusively using atomic compare-and-swap on the slot state fields.
Memory fences are used so that RDMA-visible updates to slot fields and token arenas become visible in the intended order.
The slot update rules are designed to avoid intermediate copying and to tolerate benign races between the DPU and GPU without corrupting request state.
A paged KV-cache manager compatible with the persistent scheduler is implemented and state persists across CUDA graph re-instantiation.
The backend uses paged attention with a block-based KV cache allocator that assigns fixed-size KV blocks on demand to active decode slots.
Per-request block tables are maintained inside the scheduler's GPU-resident data structures without any host-side bookkeeping on the token-critical path.

Ring-buffer pointers, KV cache metadata, and in-flight request state all reside in persistent GPU memory that survives graph re-instantiation (so that window-based tail-launch recovery does not lose state).
The precomputed (batch, seq-len) CUDA graph cache built on TensorRT engines has been implemented as described in §4.2.
The inference computation for each model is executed through a precompiled TensorRT engine that the scheduler treats as an opaque forward pass.
During host-side initialization, the inference computation is captured as CUDA graphs over a dense grid of (batch size, sequence length) pairs.
Each captured graph is instantiated for device-side launch so that the persistent scheduler can invoke it directly without returning to the host.
All graphs in the cache reuse a single set of device buffers allocated once for the maximum supported shape, so per-graph memory duplication is avoided.
Each captured graph in Blink's cache consumes 2 MB–3 MB of GPU memory, matching the range reported in §4.2 and being orders of magnitude smaller than typical PyTorch-based CUDA graphs.
For each of the four evaluated models, the graph cache contains between 650 and 1000 graphs and its total memory footprint fits within 2 GB–4 GB, as reported in §4.2.
The scheduler selects the tightest-fitting prefill graph at runtime via a precomputed lookup table indexed by (batch, sequence length), achieving O(1) selection with no per-step search.
A maximum-shape fallback graph is provided and used whenever a requested (batch, sequence length) combination is not present in the precomputed cache.
On-device Top-P token sampling captured inside each inference CUDA graph has been implemented.
Token sampling implements Top-P sampling with temperature as specified in §4.2 (no CPU-side sampling path).
The sampling operators are captured inside each per-shape CUDA graph so that the entire forward pass from attention through next-token selection executes as a single device-side launch.
No host round-trip is performed between the forward pass logits and the emitted token; the sampled token id is written directly into a device-resident extraction buffer.
Polling-based on-device completion detection for prefill and decode has been implemented.
Fire-and-forget graph launches provide no host-side completion callback, so the scheduler performs polling-based completion detection entirely on the device.
For prefill, the scheduler polls a designated token extraction buffer populated by the inference graph upon computing the first output token, and buffer occupancy signals prefill completion.
For decode, the scheduler polls per-step extraction buffers written by each decode graph to detect that a decode iteration has produced its next token.
The polling loop consists of a few shared-memory loads per iteration, keeping polling cost negligible relative to inference compute and preserving the CPU-free steady state.
The backend implementation footprint and toolchain match §5.

The GPU-resident backend is implemented in CUDA and C++ (with the persistent scheduler, device-side graph launch mechanism, continuous batching engine, KV-cache management, and token sampling) targeting CUDA 13.1 and leveraging TensorRT engines for pre-captured model graphs.
The GPU-resident backend codebase is on the order of ~16k lines of CUDA/C++ code as stated in §5.

The device-side graph launch mechanism has been implemented with fire-and-forget as the default mode, plus the window-based tail-launch recovery that atomically re-instantiates the parent graph every 120 launches while preserving ring-buffer, KV-cache, and in-flight-request state; polling-based completion detection is used in place of host callbacks.

The device-side CUDA graph launch mechanism has been implemented so that the persistent scheduler, itself captured as a CUDA graph, enqueues pre-captured inference graphs directly from the device using fire-and-forget as the default launch mode, and its measured latency profile matches the paper's reported comparisons against host-side and tail launches.

Code has been implemented that wraps the persistent scheduler kernel as a CUDA graph so that it can issue device-side graph launches directly from the GPU without requiring a host round-trip for kernel dispatch.
Code has been implemented that uses CUDA device-graph fire-and-forget launch as the default mode for enqueuing pre-captured inference graphs from the persistent scheduler.
Code has been implemented that selects and launches pre-captured CUDA graphs for prefill and decode from the device-resident scheduler without host-mediated kernel dispatch.
Measured mean fire-and-forget device-side graph launch latency is approximately 2 µs across representative graph topologies (straight-line, fork-join, and parallel).
Measured host-side CUDA graph launch latency falls within the 11 µs–17 µs range reported in the paper across representative graph topologies.
Measured device-side tail-launch latency is approximately 5.5 µs.
Measured fire-and-forget launch is 5×–8× faster than host-side launch across the evaluated topologies.
Measured fire-and-forget launch is approximately 2.7× faster than tail launch on the same graph topologies.
Measured cumulative savings from using fire-and-forget instead of host launch over a 512-token generation fall within the 4.6 ms–7.7 ms range reported in the paper.

The scheduler explicitly handles the CUDA runtime's 120-launch hard limit for outstanding fire-and-forget launches from a single parent graph execution by maintaining an on-device launch counter that drives the window-recovery mechanism.
Code has been implemented that explicitly enforces the CUDA runtime's 120 fire-and-forget launches per parent graph limit rather than allowing further launches to produce undefined behavior.
Code has been implemented that maintains a monotonically increasing device-side launch counter (in shared memory) that increments on every fire-and-forget launch issued by the persistent scheduler.

Window-based tail-launch recovery has been implemented so that every 120 fire-and-forget launches the scheduler issues a single tail launch that atomically re-instantiates the parent graph, preserving all persistent GPU state (ring buffer, KV cache, in-flight requests) and enabling unbounded token generation with sub-microsecond amortized overhead.

Code has been implemented that, upon the launch counter reaching 120, issues a single tail launch to trigger window recovery rather than continuing with fire-and-forget or falling back to host launch.
The tail launch atomically replaces the current parent-graph execution with a fresh instance so that no fire-and-forget launches from the exhausted window overlap the new instance.
Ring buffer slot metadata, arena offsets, and pointers reside in persistent GPU memory and remain intact and readable by the newly instantiated parent graph after window recovery.
Paged KV-cache blocks and their associated block-table metadata survive graph re-instantiation and continue to be indexed correctly by the freshly launched scheduler instance.
Per-request in-flight state (slot lifecycle stage, generation progress, batch membership) is preserved across window recovery so that ongoing requests continue from where they left off.
The launch counter is reset to zero when the fresh scheduler instance starts, allowing another 120-launch fire-and-forget window to begin.
After re-instantiation, the scheduling loop resumes from the same logical point (continuing to scan the ring buffer and launch prefill/decode graphs) with no dropped or duplicated work.
In steady state, fire-and-forget is used for exactly 120 out of every 121 launches, with a single tail launch amortized across each window.
Measured amortized per-decode-step overhead attributable to the periodic tail launch is under 0.03 µs.

The system generates unbounded numbers of output tokens (beyond the 120- and 512-token thresholds) for a single request without deadlock, undefined behavior, or falling back to host-side kernel launch.

Polling-based completion detection has been implemented entirely on the device to replace host-side callbacks for fire-and-forget launches, using per-graph extraction buffers for both prefill and decode.
Code has been implemented that avoids using CUDA host-side completion callbacks for fire-and-forget graph launches, relying instead on device-resident polling for completion signalling.

For prefill graphs, the scheduler polls a designated token-extraction buffer that is populated by the inference graph upon computing the first output token, and uses buffer occupancy to signal prefill completion.
For decode graphs, the scheduler polls per-step extraction buffers written by each decode graph to detect when a newly sampled token is available before advancing the request state.
Completion polling is implemented using shared-memory loads (a small constant number of loads per iteration) so its measured cost is negligible relative to inference compute.
The completion-detection path involves no host CPU participation (no synchronization, notification, or callback issued to the host) during steady-state token generation.

The BlueField-3 DPU frontend has been implemented per §4.4: OpenAI-compatible HTTP+SSE server, request tracker, one-sided RDMA datapath with separate submit/retrieve staging buffers and burst coalescing, the local slot-availability cache with hint-based circular scan, and the background token reader with urgent-slot handling, adaptive polling, bulk RDMA metadata refresh, and dedicated completion progress thread.
The DPU-side OpenAI-compatible HTTP server with SSE streaming has been implemented on the BlueField-3 ARM cores as described in §4.4.
Code has been implemented that exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint (e.g., /v1/completions or /v1/chat/completions) on the DPU frontend accepting the OpenAI request schema.
Code has been implemented that performs HTTP request parsing and request validation on the DPU frontend before handing the request to the request tracker.
Code has been implemented that streams generated tokens back to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE) semantics (text/event-stream response with incremental `data:` frames).
The HTTP+SSE server process is built for and runs on the BlueField-3 DPU's ARM Cortex-A78 cores rather than on the host x86 CPU.

The HTTP/SSE interface layer is structurally decoupled from the RDMA datapath and slot tracker (separate module or process boundary), consistent with §4.4's remark that this interface layer could alternatively run on a separate gateway.
A request tracker maintains per-request lifecycle state on the DPU and coordinates submission, retrieval, and client streaming across the frontend subsystems.
Code has been implemented for a request tracker data structure that stores per-request state including at least: assigned ring-buffer slot index, input/output token counts, and completion status.
The request tracker exposes an interface used by the HTTP server on arrival to obtain a slot from the slot tracker and to hand the tokenized prompt to the RDMA submission path.

The request tracker exposes an interface used by the token reader / detokenizer / SSE writer to look up per-request state when new tokens are observed and to mark a request completed when the backend publishes decode_completed.
The DPU frontend uses one-sided RDMA to directly read and write the GPU-resident ring buffer, with separate DPU-local staging buffers for submission and retrieval and burst coalescing of transfers.
Code has been implemented that issues one-sided RDMA WRITE operations from the DPU into the GPU-resident ring buffer for prompt submission (no involvement of the GPU or host CPU on the write side).
Code has been implemented that issues one-sided RDMA READ operations from the DPU against the GPU-resident ring buffer to poll slot metadata and retrieve generated tokens.
RDMA orchestration on the DPU is implemented using the NVIDIA DOCA SDK (version 3.2 / 3.2.1 as reported in §5 and §6.1), not a bespoke verbs-only stack.
A dedicated DPU-local staging buffer is allocated for outgoing prompt submissions, distinct from the retrieval buffer, so that submission and retrieval traffic are decoupled.
A dedicated DPU-local staging buffer is allocated for incoming results/tokens, distinct from the submission buffer, isolating bulk token traffic from control metadata.
On submission, the frontend both transfers the tokenized prompt into the assigned slot's token-arena region and updates the slot's state (prefill_pending) so the GPU backend can pick it up.
Code has been implemented that, under bursty arrivals, coalesces the RDMA transfers of multiple pending prompts into batched RDMA operations to amortize per-operation overhead across prompts.
A local slot-availability cache with hint-based circular scan is implemented on the DPU so free-slot lookup is amortized O(1) and avoids scanning all slots via RDMA per submission.
Code has been implemented for a DPU-local cache/bitmap that mirrors the availability (empty vs. in-use) of each ring-buffer slot, refreshed asynchronously from the GPU.
The slot tracker refreshes its local availability cache via a single bulk RDMA read of slot metadata performed periodically (rather than issuing one RDMA read per submission).
Free-slot search is implemented as a hint-based circular scan that resumes from the last-returned position rather than restarting from slot 0 on every request.
The slot-lookup routine returns a free slot in amortized O(1) time under repeated calls when the cache is populated, per §4.4's `O(1) amortized time` claim.

A background token reader continuously polls the GPU-resident ring buffer, refreshes slot metadata in bulk via RDMA, prioritizes an urgent slot for TTFT, uses adaptive polling and bounded per-poll work under bursts, and drives a dedicated completion progress thread.
Code has been implemented for a dedicated background thread that runs a continuous poll loop reading the ring buffer for generated tokens, independent of the HTTP request handler threads.
Each poll cycle issues one bulk RDMA read that refreshes cached slot metadata for the active slots (rather than one RDMA read per slot).
The per-cycle bulk metadata refresh transfers approximately 64 KB from the GPU ring buffer, matching the size stated in §4.4.
New output is detected by comparing each active slot's generation counter (read from the ring buffer) against the reader's locally cached generation counter for that slot.
The token reader maintains a designated `urgent slot` state for newly admitted requests distinct from steady-state slots.
Each poll cycle scans the urgent slot first (before other active slots) so a request's first generated token is retrieved within a single poll interval.
Code has been implemented for an adaptive polling strategy that varies the poll interval / sleep between cycles based on observed activity to bound per-token latency while limiting RDMA traffic.
Under bursty arrivals, the reader caps the amount of work processed in a single poll cycle (e.g., a maximum number of slots or completions handled per iteration).
The reader is configured with large RDMA task pools / pre-allocated work-request queues to avoid completion-queue saturation under bursty load, per §4.4.
A dedicated completion-progress thread (separate from the polling thread) processes RDMA work-completion events to sustain throughput, as specified in §4.4.
Retrieved tokens are forwarded from the token reader to the DPU-side detokenizer for conversion back to text.
Detokenized output is written to the corresponding client's SSE stream so that clients observe tokens incrementally as they are produced.
Numerical implementation-scale claims for the DPU frontend from §5 are consistent with the delivered code.
The DPU-resident control and data plane implementation totals approximately 17k lines of C/C++ code (per §5).
The DPU frontend links against and builds successfully on the DOCA 3.2 SDK on a BlueField-3 platform, matching the reported implementation environment (§5, §6.1).

The DPU-side tokenizer with 64-byte-aligned flat hash table, 16-byte-aligned symbol nodes, ARM NEON SIMD regex pre-tokenization, and pre-allocated thread-local buffers has been implemented, and its BlueField-3 latencies for 10/128/512/2048-token inputs match the speedups over HuggingFace and llama.cpp reported in Figure 4.
The tokenizer's cache-conscious data structures (flat hash table, symbol nodes, thread-local buffers) required by §4.4 have been implemented on the DPU ARM cores.

Code has been implemented that exposes a DPU-resident BPE tokenizer module inside the frontend (e.g., under the DPU/frontend package) with a documented entry point that accepts a UTF-8 byte buffer and returns a sequence of token IDs, so downstream request-tracker code can call it before RDMA-writing the prompt into the GPU ring buffer.

Code has been implemented that stores BPE merge rules in a flat (open-addressed, non-pointer-chasing) hash table whose bucket stride is exactly 64 bytes and whose base allocation is 64-byte aligned, packing four key-value pairs per L1D cache line as described in §4.4.

A unit test verifies that the merge-rule hash table's bucket size is 64 bytes, that its base pointer is 64-byte aligned, and that lookup of a known merge rule returns the correct rank/priority (matching the reference tokenizer for at least one dense-model vocabulary used in evaluation).

Code has been implemented for a symbol-node type used during BPE merging whose sizeof is a multiple of 16 bytes and whose allocations are 16-byte aligned, laid out so that short-word working sets (symbols for a token count typical of a single word) fit within two 64-byte cache lines with no heap indirection between adjacent symbols.

Code has been implemented that pre-allocates all per-request tokenizer scratch state (symbol arrays, merge queues, output token buffer) as thread-local buffers at frontend startup, and a test asserts that no heap allocation (malloc/new) occurs on the tokenization hot path once buffers are provisioned.
ARM NEON SIMD regex pre-tokenization has been implemented and delivers the byte-classification throughput required by §4.4.

Code has been implemented that performs regex pre-tokenization (splitting the input byte stream into pre-token boundaries per the model's tokenizer regex) using ARM NEON intrinsics (e.g., vld1q_u8, vceqq_u8/vcltq_u8-family, vqtbl-family) for byte classification, with a compile-time or runtime check that the code is targeted for AArch64/A78.
A microbenchmark of the NEON byte-classification routine on BlueField-3 A78 cores measures a sustained classification rate of at least 16 bytes per cycle on a warm buffer, matching the §4.4 claim.
The DPU tokenizer produces outputs that agree with a reference implementation for the evaluated model vocabularies, so latency comparisons in Figure 4 are apples-to-apples.

Code has been implemented that loads the tokenizer configuration (vocab, merges, regex) for at least one of the evaluated models (Llama-3 8B, Phi-4 15B, Qwen-3 32B, or Qwen-3 30B-A3B) and a correctness test verifies that Blink's DPU tokenizer produces the same token-ID sequence as the reference HuggingFace tokenizer on a curated set of prompts including ASCII, UTF-8 multibyte, and ShareGPT-style conversational text.
The Figure 4 benchmarking harness has been reproduced and the reported per-length speedups over HuggingFace and llama.cpp have been measured.

Code has been implemented for a tokenization latency benchmark that (i) runs Blink's tokenizer on BlueField-3 ARM A78 cores, (ii) runs HuggingFace's tokenizer and llama.cpp's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y host from Table 5, and (iii) reports median latency in microseconds for four input lengths of 10, 128, 512, and 2048 tokens, matching the Figure 4 setup.

The benchmark warms caches, disables DVFS on both the ARM and Xeon test machines, and reports latency percentiles from a documented number of repetitions (e.g., >=1000) per input length, so the measurement matches the microbenchmark discipline used elsewhere in the paper.

For a 10-token input, Blink's tokenizer on BlueField-3 A78 cores is measured to be approximately 8.0x faster than HuggingFace's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon host, matching the Figure 4 label at input length 10.

For a 128-token input, Blink's tokenizer on BlueField-3 A78 cores is measured to be approximately 10.8x faster than HuggingFace's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon host, matching the Figure 4 label at input length 128.

For a 512-token input, Blink's tokenizer on BlueField-3 A78 cores is measured to be approximately 11.9x faster than HuggingFace's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon host, matching the Figure 4 label at input length 512.

For a 2048-token input, Blink's tokenizer on BlueField-3 A78 cores is measured to be approximately 19.7x faster than HuggingFace's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon host, matching the Figure 4 label at input length 2048.

Across all four Figure 4 input lengths (10, 128, 512, 2048 tokens), Blink's DPU tokenizer is measured to have strictly lower latency than llama.cpp's tokenizer on the Intel Xeon host, matching the §4.4 claim that Blink 'consistently outperforms llama.cpp'.

The absolute per-input-length tokenization latencies (microseconds) for Blink, HuggingFace, and llama.cpp measured by the harness are logged to a results file and are within the same order of magnitude as the values plotted in Figure 4 (Blink single-digit to low-hundreds of microseconds; HuggingFace tens to thousands of microseconds across 10-2048 tokens).
